hints: Focus on the two different trends you need at once, how first ionisation energy changes across Period 3 and how melting point depends on structure and bonding.
Remember that first ionisation energy generally rises but dips at aluminium and at sulfur, so phosphorus ends up higher than both its neighbours.
Now compare melting points, giant structures melt very high while simple molecular P4 and S8 melt very low, and check which middle element is top for ionisation but bottom for melting.
walkthrough:
**Recall the first ionisation energy trend**

Think of first ionisation energy as how hard it is to remove the outer electron. Across Period 3 it generally increases because of increasing nuclear charge, but there are two famous dips.

Chemical definition:
$$\text{X(g)} \rightarrow \text{X}^{+}\text{(g)} + \text{e}^{-}$$

**Pin down the two dips**

Magnesium is higher than aluminium because the Al $3p$ electron is easier to remove than the Mg $3s$ electron. Phosphorus is higher than sulfur because P has a stable half-filled $3p^3$ arrangement, while S has spin-pair repulsion.

So in order: $\text{Mg} > \text{Al}$ and $\text{P} > \text{S}$.

**Recall the melting point trend**

Melting point in Period 3 is about structure. Sodium, magnesium and aluminium are metallic and rise to silicon which is giant covalent with a very high melting point. Then it drops sharply for phosphorus ($\text{P}_4$) and sulfur ($\text{S}_8$) which are simple molecular with weak van der Waals forces.

So $\text{Si}$ is very high, while $\text{P}$ and $\text{S}$ are very low, with $\text{P}$ ($44^{\circ}\text{C}$) lower than $\text{S}$ ($115^{\circ}\text{C}$).

**Find Y that is highest in IE but lowest in melting**

For silicon, phosphorus, sulfur: IE values are about Si 789, P 1012, S 1000 $\text{kJ mol}^{-1}$. So Y = phosphorus is highest because of the P > S dip. Melting points are Si 1414, P 44, S 115 $^{\circ}\text{C}$. So Y = phosphorus is also lowest. Both conditions fit perfectly.

options.A: Sodium, magnesium, aluminium fails on melting point. Y = magnesium does have the highest first ionisation energy (Mg 738 > Al 578 > Na 496), but the lowest melting point is sodium (Na 98 C, metallic with only one valence electron), not magnesium (650 C). So Y is not lowest melting.
options.B: Magnesium, aluminium, silicon fails on ionisation energy. Y = aluminium has the lowest ionisation energy of the three due to the Mg > Al dip (Si 789 > Mg 738 > Al 578). The highest is Z = silicon, not Y.
options.C: Aluminium, silicon, phosphorus fails on ionisation energy. Ionisation energy rises Al 578 < Si 789 < P 1012, so the highest is Z = phosphorus, not Y = silicon. Melting point also fails because Y = silicon (giant covalent, 1414 C) is highest, not lowest.
options.D: Silicon, phosphorus, sulfur fits both clues. For ionisation energy, P 1012 > S 1000 > Si 789, so Y = phosphorus is highest because sulfur dips below phosphorus. For melting point, Si 1414 (giant covalent) >> S 115 (S8 molecules) > P 44 (P4 molecules), so Y = phosphorus is lowest. This is the only consecutive trio where the middle element wins on IE but loses on melting.
